seo_title: Condonation of Delay Under Section 5 Limitation Act
title: Condonation of Delay Under Section 5 of the Limitation Act: What Counts as Sufficient Cause
meta_description: What a litigant must show to get a delayed appeal or application excused under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, and where courts are drawing the line now.
intro: Filing an appeal or an application a few days or a few months after limitation has expired does not automatically shut the door. Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 lets a court admit a delayed appeal or certain applications if the applicant shows sufficient cause for not filing on time, but that phrase has generated enough litigation on its own to make clear that sufficient cause is not whatever excuse the applicant finds convenient.

This guide separates what courts have actually accepted as sufficient cause from the common assumptions that turn out not to hold, including the idea that a government department gets more leeway than a private litigant, and the idea that explaining the last few days of delay is enough.

sections.heading: What Section 5 actually covers
paragraphs: Section 5 applies to appeals and to the specific applications listed in the Act; it does not apply to the filing of an original suit, where the ordinary limitation period under the Act's schedule simply runs out with no provision for a court to excuse the delay. This distinction matters because parties sometimes assume condonation is available across the board when it is, in fact, confined to the categories Section 5 names.

Where Section 5 does apply, the test is whether the applicant has shown sufficient cause for not preferring the appeal or application within the prescribed period. The provision does not define sufficient cause exhaustively, leaving courts to assess it on the facts of each case, which is why outcomes can look inconsistent from one ruling to the next even though the underlying legal test has not changed.

A court's power to condone delay under Section 5 is discretionary, not a right the applicant can claim simply by filing an application and tendering some explanation. A plausible-sounding explanation that does not actually cover the period of delay, or that reveals carelessness rather than a genuine impediment, will usually fail even if the applicant had no intention to cause harm by filing late.

sections.heading: Myth: explaining the last few days is enough
paragraphs: A recurring mistake is to explain only the final stretch before filing, for instance the time taken to get a certified copy or to brief counsel, while leaving the earlier part of the delay unaccounted for. The Supreme Court's 2025 ruling in Shivamma (Dead) by LRs v Karnataka Housing Board makes clear this will not do: sufficient cause must cover the entire period of delay, from when limitation began to run until the actual date of filing, not merely the last leg of it.

The practical effect is that an applicant has to reconstruct, and be ready to explain, what was happening at every stage between the date the cause of action or the original time limit arose and the date of actual filing. A gap in that chain, even a short one, gives the opposing side a straightforward argument that the explanation is incomplete rather than merely imperfect.

This does not mean every day has to be accounted for with forensic precision; it means the explanation has to be a continuous and credible account rather than a snapshot of the final few days dressed up as the whole story.

sections.heading: Myth: the length of the delay decides the outcome
paragraphs: Courts have repeatedly said that the length of delay, by itself, is not the decisive factor. What matters is the quality of the explanation, not the quantity of days involved. A short delay with a weak or contradictory explanation can fail where a longer delay backed by a genuine, well-documented impediment succeeds.

That said, the length of the delay is not irrelevant either; commentary on the more recent rulings notes that while it is not determinative, it remains instructive, in the sense that a very long delay naturally invites closer scrutiny of whether the explanation given is adequate to cover it. The real question courts ask is whether the applicant had a reasonable justification for not filing on time, not whether the underlying claim looks strong on its merits, though some rulings in the arbitration context have also looked at the prima facie merits as a relevant factor when weighing a Section 5 application.

Litigants should not treat a short delay as a free pass or a long delay as automatically fatal; both still need the same thing, which is a coherent account of sufficient cause covering the whole period.

sections.heading: Myth: government and public bodies get an easier standard
paragraphs: It is a common assumption that the State or a public authority, dealing with layers of internal approval and file movement, is held to a more lenient standard than a private litigant when explaining delay. The Supreme Court's Shivamma ruling pushes against that assumption directly, holding that there is no room for condoning delay caused by the lethargy or leisure of a State authority, and that institutional sluggishness is not, by itself, sufficient cause.

This followed an earlier line of authority, including Pathapati Subba Reddy v Special Deputy Collector (Land Acquisition), which also took a stricter approach to institutional delay in the land acquisition context. Together, these decisions have narrowed whatever latitude government litigants may once have enjoyed under a more liberal reading of sufficient cause.

A government department relying on internal file movement, multiple levels of sanction, or a change of counsel as the explanation for delay should expect a court today to ask for specifics: who had the file, for how long, and what each step of the process actually required, rather than accepting bureaucratic process as self-explanatory.

sections.heading: Where courts still show flexibility
paragraphs: Not every recent ruling has tightened the standard. Some 2025 decisions, including in the arbitration context, continue to describe the approach to sufficient cause as liberal, and some have factored in the apparent strength of the underlying claim when deciding whether to condone delay in that setting, which sits in some tension with the general principle that merits are not supposed to drive the Section 5 enquiry.

The safest reading for a practitioner is that the law has not swung uniformly in one direction. Courts remain more sympathetic to genuine impediments, such as documented illness, a death in the family, or a demonstrable failure of communication between a litigant and counsel that the litigant could not reasonably have prevented, than to generic claims of oversight or administrative delay, and recent rulings sharpen that distinction rather than abandon it.

An applicant filing a condonation application should therefore lead with specific, dated facts and supporting documents covering the entire delay period, rather than a general narrative, and should not assume that either a short delay or a sympathetic context will substitute for that evidence.

faqs.q: Does Section 5 of the Limitation Act apply to filing a suit late?
faqs.a: No. Section 5 applies to appeals and to the specific applications listed in the Act, not to the original filing of a suit. Once limitation for filing a suit expires, there is generally no provision allowing a court to excuse that delay.

faqs.q: Is a short delay automatically condoned?
faqs.a: No. Courts have said the length of delay is not the decisive factor; what matters is whether the explanation covers the entire period of delay credibly. A short delay with a weak or incomplete explanation can still be refused.

faqs.q: Does the government get more leeway for delay than a private party?
faqs.a: Recent Supreme Court authority, including the 2025 Shivamma ruling, says no. The Court held there is no room for excusing delay caused by a State authority's institutional lethargy, narrowing any earlier assumption that government litigants are judged more leniently.

faqs.q: What kind of explanation actually works under Section 5?
faqs.a: A continuous, dated account of what caused the delay at every stage, not just the final days before filing, supported by documents where possible. Genuine impediments such as illness or a death in the family tend to fare better than generic claims of oversight.

references: Limitation Act, 1963, Section 5 (extension of prescribed period in certain cases)
Shivamma (Dead) by LRs v Karnataka Housing Board, 2025 INSC 1104, Supreme Court (12 September 2025)
